The same platform would connect to ONPAR, Panama's asylum office, so the deportation system and the refugee protection system share one backbone. Sharma-Crawford reads it as a template. "I think this is the master plan for global implementation," she said.

What is new is the data. The platform would feed Panama's system into U.S. screening tools and a biometric repository of more than 300 million identities. Geographer Louise Amoore calls this the biometric border, a border that travels with the body itself.

A migrant who does not appeal or claim fear of return within five days is advanced automatically to removal. Immigration attorney Rekha Sharma-Crawford called it unworkable. "This window is not really a window," she said. "It's more like a trap door."

The Panama documents push this further. DHS describes a system it designed, built, funded, and can log into, operated on the ground by Panama's migration service, moving a migrant from first encounter to deportation flight in as little as five days.

Wealthy democracies have spent two decades moving their borders outward, paying other countries to stop migrants long before they reach the actual line. Scholars call it border externalization. A new DHS plan for Panama is the latest example. 🧵
